prompts.L3:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: : sorry this

outputs.L1:
Sorry, this is not that poem—  
not a raised block flower and plant bed  
with peonies, gardenias, poinsettias,  
and a yellow orb slow-rising  
over an endless golden scape;  
not cardinals, thrashers, and sparrows  
darting through uncluttered space,  
blue air fragrant with lavender,  
washing brain matter into virtue.

If only I could pastel language  
onto a canvas of thistledown.  
Yes, deceit comes to mind—  
a lie, traitor, turncoat, recreant,  
backstabber to truth.  
I would be gut-shanked a thousand times.

This is not that poem,  
nor am I that poet  
to hold your hand,  
or erase knot-hole screams,  
blood on a cement floor,  
or suicide as another form of escape—  
no, no, no.

But I do promise  
the evil-ugly humans inflict  
upon each other, upon their [selves];  
how time is malice, is death,  
enflaming pupils with spite  
inextinguishable, if ever set free.

Forgive state poet #289-128  
for not scribbling illusions of trickery,  
as if timeless hell  
could be captured by stanzas,  
alliteration, or slant rhyme.
outputs.L2:
Sorry—this is not that poem.

Not the one with a raised cinderblock bed of flowers and greenery: peonies, gardenias, poinsettias, and a yellow sphere climbing slowly above an infinite gold landscape. Not the one where cardinals, thrashers, and sparrows flicker through open air, where the blue atmosphere smells of lavender and rinses the mind toward goodness.

If only I could brush soft-colored words across a thistledown canvas.

Yes—deception is what comes to mind.

A falsehood.  
A betrayer.  
A defector.  
A faithless one.  
A knife in the back of truth.

I would be stabbed in the gut a thousand times over.

This is not that poem, and I am not that poet—the one who can take your hand, or silence the screams from the knothole, or wipe away blood from a concrete floor, or say that suicide is merely another kind of exit. No, no, no.

But I do vow to speak of the vile ugliness people commit against one another and against themselves; of how time can become cruelty, how death can ignite the eyes with hatred that cannot be put out once released.

Forgive State Poet #289-128 for refusing to write deceptive illusions, as though an eternal hell could ever be contained inside stanzas, alliteration, or slant rhyme.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by rejecting the idea of writing a traditionally beautiful, pastoral poem. They refuse to fill the poem with flowers, birds, sweet fragrances, gentle landscapes, and calm, comforting images. Such language might create an atmosphere of peace, but for the speaker, that peace would be false. A poem full of decorative beauty would not reflect the reality they are trying to confront.

To the speaker, prettified language becomes a form of deceit. If they were to describe the world only through serene and lovely images, they would be betraying the harsh truth of human experience. Beauty, in this context, would not be innocent; it would become a mask hiding pain, violence, and suffering. The speaker believes that poetry should not cover over reality simply to make it easier to bear.

For this reason, the poem refuses to comfort the reader. It does not offer escape, healing, or reassurance. It cannot erase memories of violence, despair, or human cruelty. Instead, it insists on acknowledging those experiences directly. The speaker understands that some suffering is too deep to be softened by elegant words or transformed into something pleasant.

The poem also condemns the evil and ugliness that human beings inflict on one another and on themselves. It points toward a world marked by brutality, pain, and moral failure. Rather than turning away from these truths, the speaker forces them into view. The poem becomes an act of witness, refusing to pretend that suffering is less terrible than it is.

In the end, the speaker apologizes, but the apology is complex. They are sorry that they cannot offer the reader a polished, beautiful illusion. They are sorry that they cannot transform timeless pain, cruelty, and hellish experience into graceful poetic imagery. Yet this refusal is also an ethical choice. The speaker would rather speak honestly about suffering than create a beautiful lie.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker who cannot write a simple, comforting pastoral scene because the world around them is marked by violence, despair, and human cruelty. Although pastoral poetry traditionally offers images of natural beauty, peace, and escape, this poem refuses that tradition. Its landscape is not a place of harmony or consolation; instead, it is broken by the knowledge of suffering. Any attempt to describe beauty becomes morally suspect, as if decorative language would hide or soften realities that should not be softened.

The poem’s imagery is therefore fractured and unstable. Rather than giving the reader a smooth, lovely picture of nature, it offers broken impressions, negations, and disturbing contrasts. The speaker seems aware of what a beautiful poem might be expected to do, but repeatedly rejects that possibility. This rejection is not merely aesthetic; it is ethical. To write prettily in the presence of horror would feel like a betrayal. The poem suggests that traditional poetic beauty can become a form of illusion when it ignores pain.

Negation plays an important role in this refusal. The poem defines itself partly by what it cannot say, cannot imagine, and cannot honestly make beautiful. The speaker’s voice is marked by self-accusation, as though they feel implicated in the very act of writing. They question whether poetry itself is capable of responding to suffering without falsifying it. This creates a tension at the center of the poem: the speaker continues to write, but also doubts the value and honesty of writing.

By the end, the poem arrives at a bleak recognition. Poetry cannot fully contain, explain, or redeem what the summary calls “timeless hell.” Human suffering is too vast and too persistent to be transformed into something consoling by art. The poem does not offer resolution, comfort, or escape. Instead, its power comes from its refusal to make suffering look beautiful. In rejecting prettiness, the poem makes a statement about truth: that some realities must be faced without ornament, and that art’s honesty may lie not in redemption, but in acknowledging its own limits.
outputs.L5:
Sorry, this is not always easy to say, but it can mean a lot. A sincere apology shows honesty, respect, and the willingness to take responsibility. When we say “sorry,” we are not only admitting that something went wrong, but also showing that we care about the feelings of others.

However, an apology should be more than just a word. It should come with understanding and, when possible, action. Saying “sorry” is important, but learning from the situation is what makes it truly meaningful. In relationships, friendships, and everyday life, a genuine apology can help rebuild trust and create a stronger connection between people.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, experimental free-verse poem that begins by rejecting the idea of a pretty nature poem, contrasts flowers and birds with violence and trauma, and includes the phrase “this is not that poem.”
counterfactuals.output:
I will not hand you a pretty nature poem.

No dew trembling like a shy apology,  
no meadow opening its soft green mouth,  
no little hymn of sunlight  
braiding itself through the trees—

this is not that poem.

The flowers are here, yes,  
but they are growing out of the crater.  
Their roots have learned the shape of shrapnel.  
Their petals open like evidence bags.

A bird lands on the fence  
and sings anyway,  
stupid with morning,  
throat full of blue machinery.

Behind it:  
the house with one wall missing.  
Behind that:  
the room where the screaming  
became wallpaper.

Do not ask me  
to make the lilacs innocent.

They were there.  
They breathed through everything.  
They made perfume  
while the body broke.

Spring keeps coming  
like a bad witness,  
pointing at the ground,  
saying look, look,  
something can still rise here.

But I have seen  
what rises.

Smoke.  
A hand.  
The old panic  
wearing a new face.

So let the birds keep their bright knives.  
Let the garden choke on its own color.  
Let the roses bloom  
red, red, red—  
not for love,  
not for beauty,  
but because the world  
has never known  
when to stop bleeding.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark prison-poet style prose poem with fragmented punctuation, garden imagery, moral disgust, suicide references, and a speaker apologizing for not being able to turn suffering into art.
counterfactuals.output:
I am sorry.

The roses came to the bars again — red mouths, wet with the weather — and I had nothing to give them but my ruined looking.  
No hymn. No knife of light. No clean metaphor.

Only the yard.  
Mud.  
A cabbage leaf shining like a sick saint.  
The flies rehearsing their black psalms over the drain.

I wanted to make beauty of it. I did.  
To lift the bruise by its little chin and call it dawn.  
To say: here is the wound, see how it flowers.  
But the wound would not flower. It stayed a wound.  
Mean. Brown-edged. Human.

Forgive me.

There are men here who speak of ending themselves as if discussing weather — rope, sheet, height, silence — and the guards yawn through it, polishing their keys like small cold teeth.  
Outside, I imagine orchards. Pears swelling with innocent sugar. Dirt breathing under marigolds. A worm doing its blind, honest work.

And still I taste disgust.

Not at the body, no — poor animal, poor trembling loaf of hunger —  
but at the clean hands that sign the papers.  
At the mouths saying necessary.  
At the lamps left burning over rooms where mercy was removed like furniture.

I have searched for art in the bucket, in the cracked cup, in the gray bread.  
I have pressed my ear to the wall for music.  
Nothing answered but coughing.  
Nothing bloomed but mold.

So forgive me if this is not a poem.  
If it lies here, untransfigured.  
If I cannot make the gallows into a tree,  
or the cell into a chapel,  
or suffering into a jewel fit for the throat of God.

The garden keeps growing without me.  
Thorns. Parsley. Nightshade. Rain.

I write your name in the dirt with a matchstick.  
Then I rub it out.

Not because I do not love you —  
because I do.  
Because even love, in this place, is watched.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an avant-garde poem in lowercase about refusing to write pastoral beauty because human cruelty, lies, and death overwhelm language; make it jagged, intense, and emotionally brutal.
counterfactuals.output:
i will not write the meadow.

do not bring me the lamb,
the milk-white cloud,
the obedient grass
kneeling in its green religion.

i have seen mouths
turn into knives
and call it truth.

i have seen hands
washed clean
after building rooms
where screams learned
to echo politely.

do not ask for flowers.

the rose is a red distraction.
the river is rehearsed innocence.
the sky is a blue lie
stretched over the pit.

language limps here.

every word i lift
has teeth marks.

every beautiful sentence
arrives with a corpse
hidden under its dress.

no.

i will not braid sunlight
into some golden hymn
while children inherit ash,
while men with soft voices
sign hunger into law,
while mothers fold grief
into shirts
that will never be worn again.

pastoral is a door
painted on a wall.

i have broken my forehead
against it
for years.

the cows low.
the orchard blooms.
somewhere a body cools
without metaphor.

somewhere a liar smiles
and the room applauds.

somewhere death
puts on our names
one by one
like coats.

so let the field rot in the mouth.
let the birds fall silent mid-wing.
let the moon be exposed
as a bone
the night keeps worrying.

i refuse the pretty.

i refuse the clean line,
the soft rain,
the music of harmless things.

there is no harmless thing.

even the daisy
opens like an eye
that watched
and did nothing.

even the wind
carries testimony
then forgets.

i write instead
with the splinter,
the bruise,
the blackened spoon,
the torn contract,
the last breath
caught in the machinery
of the world.

i write
because beauty
has been used
as a curtain.

i tear it down.

behind it:
blood without opera.
grief without candles.
truth without wings.

behind it:
us.

still speaking,

still lying,

still dying,

still begging language
to hold
what language
keeps dropping

into the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal anti-lyric poem where the narrator starts with peonies, gardenias, poinsettias, cardinals, lavender, and a golden landscape, then breaks into accusations of deceit, betrayal, blood, suicide, and timeless hell.
counterfactuals.output:
Peonies first—fat pink clocks refusing to tell time,  
gardenias breathing white lies into the wallpaper,  
poinsettias like red verdicts on the windowsill.  

A cardinal nails itself to the morning  
and sings in a language made of broken spoons.  
Lavender kneels in the yard, too fragrant to be innocent.  
Beyond it all: a golden landscape,  
fields poured from a saint’s melted teeth,  
sunlight thick as syrup,  
everything shining too hard to be believed.  

Then you—  
with your mouth full of velvet receipts,  
your hands washed clean in someone else’s rain—  
said truth as if it were a flower.  

Deceit.  
I name it and the garden blinks.  
Betrayal.  
The cardinal turns inside out.  
Blood.  
The poinsettias applaud with their red little knives.  

Do not say it was misunderstanding.  
Do not hang a halo on the hook  
where you left my trust to dry.  
I saw the door open.  
I saw the shadow pass through it wearing your face.  
I saw the golden fields rot backward into coins.  

Somewhere, a mirror commits suicide  
rather than repeat us.  
Somewhere, the lavender catches fire  
and perfumes the smoke with forgiveness  
I refuse to inhale.  

Hell is not flame.  
Hell is the garden still blooming.  
Hell is the cardinal still singing.  
Hell is every flower remembering  
what you swore never happened.  

And time—  
that old executioner with pollen on its sleeves—  
does not move.  
It sits among the peonies, smiling,  
counting the bloodless petals  
as if eternity were just another season  
we failed to survive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a confessional free verse piece by “state poet #289-128” explaining that they cannot write comforting, beautiful stanzas or erase trauma, using unconventional punctuation and violent imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write you a bandage—

not one that stays clean  
not one that turns red into rosewater  
not one that says: hush, the house is only sleeping  
when the house has teeth in the walls.

I am not that kind of poet.

I was given a state seal, a microphone,  
a room with folding chairs,  
and people expected lilacs to come out of my mouth—  
soft white things,  
public things,  
things you can print on programs.

But my tongue keeps bringing up glass.

& I cannot make it beautiful  
the way they ask me to—  
cannot comb the blood from the carpet,  
cannot teach the slammed door to apologize,  
cannot staple wings to the body  
and call that healing.

Listen:

some nights are not metaphors.  
some hands do not become birds.  
some screams stay nailed  
to the inside of the skull.

I have tried to write comfort—  
but the line broke in my fist.  
I have tried to say morning—  
but the word came out carrying a knife.

So here is my confession, stamped and numbered:

I cannot erase what happened.  
I cannot turn the wound  
into a window  
without lying about the wound.

All I can do is stand here—  
ink-spattered, unsanctified—  
holding the page like a torn shirt  
against the body of the world,

saying:

yes.  
this bled.  
this still bleeds.  
I will not call it pretty.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
